title: Immune signals and chronic pain
objective: Connect sustained immune signaling to chronic sensitization and the lab's disease models.

steps.title: When the loop won't quit
steps.body: Sustained immune signaling keeps neurons sensitized — contributing to [[peripheral sensitization|peripheral]] and [[central sensitization]] and, in the viscera, to [[visceral hypersensitivity]]. This is why inflammatory gut disease so often comes with pain that outlasts the tissue damage.

steps.prompt: Why does pain in inflammatory conditions often persist and spread?
options: Ongoing immune signaling sustains peripheral and central sensitization
The nerves have been permanently cut by the inflammation itself
Pain pathways shut down entirely for the duration of inflammation
The original tissue damage never fully heals in these conditions
steps.explanation: As long as immune signals keep sensitizing neurons (peripherally and centrally), the pain is maintained and can spread — a self-sustaining neuroimmune state.

variants.reveal: Continued immune signaling keeps neurons sensitized, maintaining pain.

steps.setup: In a colitis model, you silence the sensitized visceral afferents during active inflammation.
steps.prompt: What do you predict for hypersensitivity?
options: It should drop if those afferents carry it
Nothing, if the hypersensitivity is maintained in the spinal cord
steps.reveal: Silencing the afferents tests whether they carry the immune-driven hypersensitivity — the neuroimmune version of the loss-of-function experiment the lab runs (and it links straight to A9).

variants.prompt: Silencing sensitized gut afferents in colitis should…
options: Lower the hypersensitivity, if they drive it
Change only the conduction speed, nothing else
variants.explanation: Loss-of-function tests whether those afferents carry the hypersensitivity.

sources.citation: Wallrapp A & Chiu IM, 2024, Annu Rev Immunol
sources.note: Review of bidirectional neuroimmune interactions in the intestine.

reviewNotes: Immune-driven chronic sensitization; ties A9 + lab models.
